content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to perturb the feature map adversarially to improve domain generalization (RASP). To balance the style perturbations with original features, the normalized feature mixup (NFM) is proposed. RASP and NFM are equipped before and after each residual block. The extensive experiments on several datasets verify the effectiveness of the method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
+ Interesting idea to use adversarial feature perturbations for domain adaptation.
+ The proposed method significantly increases the performance from state of the art.
+ The paper is easy to follow and implement with (promised) available codes

Weakness
+ My major concern is how Alg 1 works in the overall training. Does each block conduct RASP optimization for (at most) T times before entering the next block, or a backward propagation simultaneously optimize all blocks? The former is very time-consuming and the latter is also not efficient. In this regard, it would be necessary to report the computation amount when compared with baselines. (But it is good that the method does not increase inference time)
+ The motivation of NFM is not clear. Although it is said that pure RASP does not work well, is it possible to reduce the style perturbations, e.g., by decreasing T or increasing \tao? The condition (10) is also heuristically designed, which may not be necessary when T is set.
+ Could the method be applied to architectures besides ResNets? For example, inception, densenet, ViT.
+ (8)(9) are neither $\ell_\infty$ nor $\ell_2$ optimization. Is it suitable to update features with sign gradients? Because features are not like images with discrete pixel values.
+ The thresholding ablation study does not clearly reflect the trend. Better results may be achieved by t=0.9 given the presented monotonous trend.
content.summary_of_the_review: The method achieves great results, but the paper fails to illustrate important parts of the key processes and motivation.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the domain generalization problem. This paper proposes a data augmentation method, to let the model see images from different domains. Those images are generated by a stylized adversarial attack method – generate difficult images by changing its style. The experiments were conducted on several datasets, and show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

Authors conducted the experiments on several datasets and showed promising results.
This paper is well-written and easy to follow. The high-level idea is clear and easy to understand. Overall the proposed method is simple but effective.

Weakness

If I understand correctly, adversarial attack is only one method to obtain OOD images for training. There are other methods that can also generate images with different styles (eg, random perturb the mean and std instead of attack). This ablation might be interesting.

In section 4.2, the author mentioned that each model is trained for 30 epochs. Wondering if the results can improve if training longer.

The baseline seems weak and some related work is not discussed, eg [a]. It would be good if some state-of-the-art methods can be discussed. If I understand correctly, you could find some state-of-the-art methods [here](https://paperswithcode.com/sota/domain-generalization-on-domainnet), [here](https://paperswithcode.com/sota/domain-generalization-on-office-home) and [here](https://paperswithcode.com/sota/domain-generalization-on-pacs-2).


[a] Rangwani, Harsh, et al. "A closer look at smoothness in domain adversarial training." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Good. I can easily follow the idea.

Quality: seems good expect I am not sure if related works and baselines are fully discussed.

Originality: cannot judged because related works are not fully discussed. [a] seems also use adversarial training to do domain adaption. It would be good to discuss them if related.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea is interesting and the results look to be effective. However, my most concerns is the related works are not fully discussed. I am not familiar with domain generalization, but according to search I see some stronger results in paperswithcode.com. Some of those methods are published but not discussed. Therefore, if those papers are related, it would be good to discuss them as well.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper tackles domain generalization using an approach based on randomized adversarial style perturbations. The method is motivated by the observation reported in previous work (i.e., MixStyle) that feature statistics capture style (domain) information.

The method has two components. The first component injects adversarial gradients computed using random labels into feature statistics for style augmentation. The second component mixes the augmented features with the original features via Mixup. The method is found to be effective on three domain generalization benchmarks, i.e., DomainNet, PACS and OfficeHome.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

Since the introduction of MixStyle in domain generalization, several follow-up works have attempted to augment feature style in different ways. But the idea proposed in this work—which is based on adversarial gradients—is new. The idea could be useful for those working on feature statistics-based methods. The results show that the method beats current SOTA feature statistics-based method, StyleNeophile, which is encouraging.

**Weaknesses**

The reviewer has some concerns and feels that the impact of this work might be limited. Please see below for the detailed comments.

1. The first step of the method is to augment feature style using adversarial gradients, which makes sense. But the second step that brings the features back to the original style is confusing and contradicts with the motivation. This needs more explanation and evidence. The contribution would be made more significant if the paper shows using the adversarial gradients is more effective than other feature statistics-based methods. What are the results of using the RASP module alone, i.e., the main contribution? This piece of information is missing in the paper.

2. The ablation results shown in Table 4 aren't well organized, making it hard for readers to extract information about how much improvement the NFM module brings. Is it about 1\% increase in performance on average?

3. MixStyle, which is a very relevant method, isn't compared on DomainNet.

4. In terms of the design, it's odd to have a two-stream architecture where the perturbation-free and perturbation-based streams need to be run in parallel. The design isn't efficient and thus might have minimal impact in practical applications.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**: The paper is generally easy to follow.

**Quality**: The motivation is clear, relevant papers are properly discussed in the related work, the method makes sense, and the results look good overall.

**Novelty**: The idea of injecting adversarial gradients to feature statistics is new to feature statistics-based methods but the main idea of augmenting feature statistics is based on previous work (i.e., MixStyle).

**Reproducibility**: The implementation detail has been provided in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed idea of injecting adversarial gradients to feature statistics is new but the paper lacks more in-depth explanations and some ablation results, which make the contributions limited.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed an easy and effective method to solve the domain adaptation problem. It borrows the attack idea from adversarial examples. Instead of attacking input images, this work tries to attack channel-wise mean and standard deviation, which creates a more diverse augmentation in the style space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. This paper is clear-written, and I enjoyed reading it. The authors introduced many related works and analyzed the difference between this paper and others.
2. It is interesting to know that merely attacking mean and standard deviation could achieve such impressive performance. I appreciate this simple and novel idea.
3. Experiments are solid and well defended their statements.

Weaknesses:
1. Why not do some experiments on a standard dataset, such as ImageNet? It seems this method could be regarded as a data augmentation method, and I am curious whether this method will drop accuracy on clean data.
2. What will the results be if we directly add this method to the previous SOTA? Will combining them result in a new SOTA?
3. If the authors can show some perturbated images, that will be interesting.
4. Could the authors explain why this simple method outperforms previous generative-model-based methods? I am not sure why generative-model-based methods cannot produce a more diverse augmentation in the style space.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I like this idea and think it is reproducible, and the authors promise that they will release the code.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is solid and puts forward an interesting domain adaptation method. I recommend accepting it.

content.title: Randomized Adversarial Style Perturbations for Domain Generalization
content.abstract: While deep neural networks have shown remarkable progress in various computer vision tasks, they often suffer from weak generalization ability on unseen domains. To tackle performance degradation under such domain shifts, Domain Generalization (DG) aims to learn domain invariant features applicable to unseen target domains based only on the data in source domains. This paper presents a simple yet effective approach for domain generalization via style perturbation using adversarial attacks. Motivated by the observation that the characteristics of each domain are captured by the feature statistics corresponding to style, we propose a novel domain generalization technique, referred to as Randomized Adversarial Style Perturbations (RASP). The proposed algorithm augments the styles of features to deceive the network outputs towards randomly selected labels during training and prevents the network from being misled by the unexpected styles observed in unseen target domains. While RASP is effective to handle domain shifts, its naïve integration into the training procedure might degrade the capability of learning knowledge from source domains because it has no restriction on the perturbations of representations. This challenge is alleviated by Normalized Feature Mixup (NFM), which facilitates learning the original features while achieving robustness to perturbed representations via their mixup during training. We evaluate the proposed algorithm via extensive experiments on various benchmarks and show that our approach improves domain generalization ability, especially in large-scale benchmarks.
